cycle_time.insight: Cycle time is fairly predictable for the middle of the distribution, but a long tail of slow items makes the team less reliable for anything outside the typical flow. The improving trend suggests the system is getting faster overall, yet the spread and outliers mean stakeholders should still plan with a wide safety margin for complex work. Variation by type is real: bugs are usually fast when they finish, but their mean is pulled up by slower cases, while user stories show a higher median than backlog items.
evidence: weekly trend slope -0.14 days/week, trend improving
Bug mean 16.1 days vs median 5.7; User Story median 10.1 days
cycle_time.watch_out: Check whether the longest items are tied to blockers, rework, or specific item classes rather than normal delivery.

lead_time.insight: Stakeholders can usually expect items to take around two weeks from start to finish, but the mean is much higher because a smaller set of very slow items is stretching the distribution. The widening gap between lead time and cycle time suggests waiting before work starts is a major driver, not just slow execution once work begins. The worsening trend means planning confidence is deteriorating even while active delivery remains reasonably fast.
evidence: median lead time 12.1 days vs mean 36.7 days
median lead time 12.1 days vs median cycle time 7.0 days
weekly trend slope 1.85 days/week, trend worsening
lead_time.watch_out: Investigate queueing before development and any very old items that are distorting stakeholder expectations.

throughput.insight: Delivery is broadly steady enough for rough forecasting, with no zero-completion weeks and a modest upward trend over the window. That said, the weekly swings are large enough that the team still behaves in batches at times rather than as a perfectly smooth flow system. The improving trend is encouraging, but the variability means forecasts should still be treated as ranges, not promises.
evidence: 87 items completed over 13 weeks, 6.7 per week on average
throughput.watch_out: Look for batching around release/testing cycles that may still cause completion spikes.

time_in_columns.insight: Refinement is the clearest accumulation point, taking far longer than any other step and suggesting a queueing or prioritisation bottleneck before development. In-progress time is also substantial, so the constraint is not purely upstream; once work starts, it is not flowing quickly enough either. If Refinement were shortened materially, cycle time would likely improve, but only if downstream work can absorb the flow.
evidence: Ready For Test, In Test, and Ready for Release are all much lower than Refinement
time_in_columns.watch_out: Confirm whether Refinement is overloaded because too much work enters it, or because items sit there waiting for decisions, dependencies, or review.

flow_efficiency.insight: Most items spend far more time waiting than actively being worked on, which points to a low-efficiency flow system. The median of 0% shows many items have almost no active-touch time relative to total elapsed time, while the high tail indicates a smaller set does get worked efficiently. Improving this would require reducing queue time and handoff delay, not just asking people to work faster.
flow_efficiency.watch_out: See whether low-efficiency items cluster in specific columns, types, or blocked states.

work_start_efficiency.insight: Once items are committed, they usually start development quickly, so the main problem is not deciding to begin work after commitment. The long average wait before development is being skewed by a smaller set of items that sit for a long time before starting. That suggests queue management and selection discipline matter more than execution discipline at the start of work.
work_start_efficiency.watch_out: Inspect the low-efficiency items to see whether they were deliberately deferred, blocked by dependencies, or simply left idle.

wip.insight: WIP is high enough to create multitasking overhead and is likely suppressing flow. Most inventory sits in Refinement and In Progress, which means the team is carrying work before it is finished rather than keeping items moving to completion. Reducing WIP should improve cycle time by shortening queues and freeing focus.
evidence: Refinement has 13 items; In Progress has 9
WIP trend slope 1.13 per week, trend increasing
wip.watch_out: Check whether the growing WIP is caused by more intake, slower finishing, or both.

wip_over_time.insight: WIP has been trending upward over the period, which suggests work is accumulating faster than it is being cleared. The swings from low 20s to 40 indicate the team is not keeping a consistently bounded system. That pattern usually means WIP is being managed reactively rather than actively controlled.
evidence: weekly WIP rises from 20 to 40 in the window
wip_over_time.watch_out: Find the weeks where WIP jumped most and correlate them with starts, blockers, and release activity.

wip_age_distribution.insight: The age profile is heavily skewed toward older work, with a large share of items already over two weeks old and many past a month. That means ageing work is not an exception; it is a meaningful part of the current system. A dominant old-age band suggests the team is tolerating work that is unlikely to finish quickly unless something changes.
evidence: median age 26.8 days, average age 54.9 days
14 of 34 WIP items are over 30 days old
wip_age_distribution.watch_out: Identify whether the oldest items are blocked, stalled in review, or simply low priority.

wip_age_by_column.insight: The oldest items are concentrated in Refinement, Ready, and In Progress, with especially severe outliers in Refinement and Ready for Release. The wide gap between median and p85 within columns suggests this is partly a systemic ageing problem and partly a small number of extreme outliers. Downstream stages are not the only issue; upstream queueing is also contributing.
evidence: Ready for Release p85 198.0 days, max 198.0 days
wip_age_by_column.watch_out: Check whether the longest-lived items share dependencies, ownership gaps, or lack of explicit decision dates.

blockers.insight: Blocking is costing the system real time, with more than 100 days lost across the currently blocked set. The blocked items are concentrated in Backlog and In Progress, which suggests both intake-side and execution-side dependency management issues. The pattern looks persistent rather than episodic, so blockers are probably a structural part of the current workflow.
evidence: blocked by column: Backlog 1, In Progress 2
blockers.watch_out: Confirm whether blocked items are waiting on external teams, unclear requirements, or internal decision points.

blocked_by_signal.insight: Blocking is dominated by the generic 'Blocked' signal, with a small secondary signal for external dependency waiting. That indicates most impediments are being recorded as hard blocks rather than a wide mix of categories. The relatively narrow signal distribution suggests the team may be under-classifying the real cause of delay.
evidence: one signal category accounts for most blocked items
blocked_by_signal.watch_out: Check whether the team is using the blocked tag consistently and whether root causes are being captured separately.

blockers_by_column.insight: Blocked items are concentrated in the work-execution area rather than only before work starts. With two blocked items already in progress and one in backlog, the pattern points to both demand-side and delivery-side interference. The in-progress concentration suggests blockers are interrupting active delivery, not just preventing starts.
evidence: currently blocked items include 2 in progress and 1 in backlog
blockers_by_column.watch_out: See whether blocked in-progress items are waiting on cross-team input, environment issues, or rework.

blocker_timeline.insight: Blocking has been present throughout the whole window and has ticked up recently, so it does not look like a one-off incident. The weekly counts stay low and flat for much of the period, then increase to 4 in the final two observed weeks. That makes blocking look more structural than random.
evidence: blocked counts appear in all 13 weeks
Blocked signal rises to 4 in 2026-07-30 and 2026-08-06
blocker_timeline.watch_out: Distinguish between brief pauses and genuinely prolonged block states, especially in the latest weeks.

days_lost_to_blockers.insight: Blocking is not a minor interruption for the items that experience it; for some, blocked time is a very large share of in-progress time. One item is effectively entirely consumed by blocked time, which indicates a structural dependency rather than a brief delay. This pattern implies that removing blockers could materially shorten delivery time for affected work.
evidence: currently blocked item 497159 has 938.0 days blocked
blocked items 1240649 and 1240654 each have 8.1 days blocked
total blocked days 106.2 across 3 currently blocked items
days_lost_to_blockers.watch_out: Compare blocked duration to total elapsed time for each blocked item to see whether blockers are the dominant delay mode or an occasional pause.

stale_work.insight: There is a small but important set of untouched or long-unchanged items, mostly bugs and backlog work. That suggests backlog hygiene is not strong enough to keep old work visible and either revived or removed. Stale items reduce planning accuracy because they inflate the apparent pool of available work without indicating real readiness.
evidence: 5 stale items over 30 days since update
3 of the stale items are bugs
2 stale items sit in Backlog with New state
stale_work.watch_out: Check whether stale backlog items are still valid priorities or should be closed, re-triaged, or re-estimated.

net_flow.insight: The system is currently completing slightly more than it receives, so it is not obviously overrun at the whole-board level. But the week-to-week swings show the margin is thin and not yet stable enough to call the flow sustainable with confidence. The delivery risk is improving overall, but the volatility means the system can still slip into buildup quickly.
evidence: weekly net flow ranges from -6 to +7
net_flow.watch_out: Watch whether recent high-completion weeks are real capacity gains or just clearing accumulated work.

arrival_departure.insight: The board is broadly balanced column by column, so there is no single stage where arrivals persistently exceed departures. That means the current congestion is more likely coming from local queues and ageing work than from a simple arrival-departure mismatch in one step. Improvement effort should therefore focus on the specific slow columns rather than trying to tune the entire board equally.
arrival_departure.watch_out: Use this alongside ageing and WIP data, because balance alone does not rule out a slow queue.

bugs.insight: Bug completions are happening, but the overall bug picture is not yet clearly shrinking because creations and completions are close enough that small spikes can reverse progress. Open bugs remain substantial, and the backlog of bugs is concentrated in the early pipeline. That means bug handling is active, but not yet cleanly continuous or fully absorbing incoming defect demand.
evidence: bug completions by week include a spike to 6 in 2026-08-03
28 of 34 open bugs are in Backlog
bugs.watch_out: Track whether the recent completion spike is enough to reduce the backlog or just temporary catch-up.

bug_intake.insight: Bug intake is uneven and shows clear spike weeks, especially late in the window. Creations are close to completions over the full period, but the recent spikes suggest defect inflow can surge around delivery events. That pattern can build quality debt if the team only resolves bugs in bursts rather than as part of steady flow.
evidence: bug creations also rise to 4 in 2026-06-22
bug creations total across the window is near completions, but late spikes are visible
bug completions and creations both spike in the same late period
bug_intake.watch_out: Correlate bug spike weeks with releases, incidents, or major feature launches.

bug_pct.insight: Bugs are a non-trivial share of the active system, so they are competing with feature work for capacity. Because the bug share is concentrated in backlog rather than active stages, the immediate issue is less about firefighting than about triage and prioritisation. If that share grows, feature capacity will be squeezed further.
evidence: 34 open bugs out of 629 total bugs tracked
only 1 open bug is in In Progress
bug_pct.watch_out: Monitor whether bug share shifts from backlog into active columns, which would indicate higher interruption cost.

bug_net_flow.insight: Across the period the team is close to balancing bug creation and resolution, but the bursts imply that any small slowdown could quickly create a backlog. The late surge in completions is encouraging, yet it may be catch-up rather than sustained burn-down. The quality debt trajectory therefore looks fragile rather than clearly improving.
evidence: bug completions total is close to bug creations over the window
bug_net_flow.watch_out: Look for consecutive weeks where bug completions stay above creations, not just single-week spikes.

bug_distribution.insight: Most open bugs are still untriaged in Backlog, with only a small number reaching active delivery stages. That suggests the bug management problem is primarily triage and prioritisation, not execution capacity in test or release. The small number in downstream columns means QA/release is not currently the main bug pile-up point.
evidence: 1 open bug in Ready for Release
bug_distribution.watch_out: Check whether backlog bugs are being intentionally parked or are simply awaiting ownership and severity decisions.

cfd.insight: The cumulative flow looks broadly smooth, but the growing accumulation signal shows the system is carrying more work than it is clearing over time. The CFD does not show a dramatic widening between any single pair of columns, which aligns with the arrival/departure balance chart rather than contradicting it. That points to dispersed congestion and ageing rather than one obvious transition failure.
evidence: arrival rate per week 11.9 vs departure rate 9.6
average items per column are highest in Backlog and Refinement
cfd.watch_out: Use the CFD with ageing and WIP to see whether accumulation is hidden in a queue rather than visible as a band widening.

wip_level_distribution.insight: Some columns regularly operate near or above their limits, especially In Progress and Ready for Release, while In Test is often empty and therefore not a constraint. The pattern suggests the limits are not equally calibrated across the board: a few stages are structurally pressured while others have spare capacity. Where the modal level is near or above the limit, the issue looks systemic rather than occasional.

diagnostic_findings.finding: The primary constraint appears to be upstream queueing and refinement, with downstream work also affected.
evidence: Refinement mean 304.9 hours vs other columns far lower

diagnostic_findings.interpretation: The team usually starts items quickly once committed, but many items spend a long time waiting before or around refinement and development. That suggests the biggest loss is in queue management and prioritisation before active execution, not only in execution speed.
plausible_explanations: Too much work is entering refinement without enough decision capacity
Dependencies or unclear acceptance criteria are leaving items parked
The team is starting more items than it can finish, which creates upstream backlog
Review/release constraints are feeding back into earlier stages

diagnostic_findings.finding: Flow is batchy enough that simple averages overstate day-to-day predictability.

WIP ranges from 20 to 40 over the window

Test/release or dependency checkpoints create pulses
Small team size or context switching amplifies weekly volatility
A few very old items distort average lead and cycle measures

diagnostic_findings.finding: WIP appears high relative to throughput, which is consistent with slower flow and ageing work.

median WIP age 26.8 days with 14 items over 30 days old

Work is trapped in queues between stages
The board includes large numbers of low-priority or dormant items
Capacity is being split across too many classes of work

diagnostic_findings.finding: Blocking is a structural issue, not an isolated exception.

Blocked states are used inconsistently and items remain blocked too long
Decision ownership is unclear for some work
The team lacks a fast path for unblocking critical items

Ownership for old backlog items is unclear

diagnostic_findings.finding: Quality work is present but managed mostly as backlog inventory rather than active flow.
evidence: bug creations and completions are close over the window but spike late

Feature pressure is crowding out bug handling
Bug severity is being downgraded or parked
A recent delivery spike temporarily increased defect intake

executive_summary.headline: The team is delivering steadily overall, but too much work is waiting too long in queues, especially in refinement and early delivery stages.
executive_summary.narrative: Work is getting finished often enough to keep delivery moving, but a lot of it is sitting around before it is truly ready or while it is waiting for decisions and dependencies. The oldest items are not isolated exceptions; they are spread through the system, and some have been there for months. A few blocked items are consuming far more time than they should, which points to a dependency management problem rather than occasional bad luck. Bugs are being handled, but mostly as backlog inventory rather than a smooth stream of active work. Overall, the system looks more constrained by queueing and ageing than by raw execution speed.
executive_summary.primary_diagnosis: The system is constrained mainly by upstream queueing and ageing work, with blocking and late-stage delays reinforcing the slowdown.
executive_summary.main_caveat: The data shows strong patterns, but it does not prove the exact root cause of the queues without item-level context on ownership, dependencies, and prioritisation decisions.

recommendations.action: Reduce work entering Refinement by tightening intake and limiting concurrent items there.
recommendations.why: Refinement is the strongest bottleneck and holds the most accumulated work, so lowering its load should reduce queue time.
recommendations.first_step: Set a hard cap on new items entering Refinement for one iteration and review the items already there.
recommendations.metric_to_watch: Refinement time in column, WIP in Refinement, cycle time
recommendations.expected_effect: Shorter waiting time before development and lower end-to-end cycle time.

recommendations.action: Introduce an explicit unblock escalation path with ownership and due dates.
recommendations.why: Blocking is persistent and expensive, so items need faster resolution than passive waiting.
recommendations.first_step: Create a daily review of all blocked items with one named owner and a next action for each.
recommendations.expected_effect: Fewer days lost to blockers and fewer extremely old blocked items.

recommendations.action: Lower active WIP, especially in In Progress and Refinement.
recommendations.why: WIP is high relative to throughput, which is consistent with multitasking overhead and ageing.
recommendations.first_step: Agree a temporary cap reduction and stop starting new work when the cap is reached.
recommendations.metric_to_watch: current_wip, wip_over_time, cycle_time median and p85
recommendations.expected_effect: Less ageing, better flow efficiency, and more predictable completions.

recommendations.action: Run a backlog hygiene and triage sweep for stale items and old bugs.
recommendations.why: Stale work is distorting planning and keeping low-value items alive.
recommendations.first_step: Review every item older than 30 days without updates and either re-own, re-prioritise, or close it.
recommendations.expected_effect: Cleaner queue, better planning accuracy, fewer dormant items.

recommendations.action: Reserve a small, regular capacity slice for bug handling instead of relying on batch catch-up.
recommendations.why: Bug work is concentrated in backlog and resolves in bursts, which risks quality debt.
recommendations.first_step: Allocate a fixed weekly bug triage/fix slot and limit how many bugs can wait unowned.
recommendations.expected_effect: More continuous bug burn-down and less backlog accumulation.

recommendations.action: Review release-readiness steps and remove avoidable manual gates.
recommendations.why: Ready for Release items can age significantly, so late-stage friction is likely contributing to delay.
recommendations.first_step: Map the steps required for release-ready items and identify any recurring approval or coordination waits.
recommendations.metric_to_watch: time in Ready for Release, p85 age in Ready for Release
recommendations.expected_effect: Faster movement through the final stage and lower tail latency.

recommendations.action: Forecast using percentile ranges, not just averages.
recommendations.why: Lead time and throughput are variable enough that averages alone will mislead planning.
recommendations.first_step: Communicate a median and p85 delivery expectation for common work types.
recommendations.metric_to_watch: lead_time median vs p85, cycle_time median vs p85
recommendations.expected_effect: More realistic stakeholder expectations and fewer missed commitments.

data_quality_caveats: The window is only 3 months, so some patterns may be temporary or influenced by recent events.
Several metrics have long tails and extreme outliers, which inflate means relative to medians.
The summary is anonymised and item-level context such as ownership, dependency chains, and release events is missing.
Blocked and stale data may reflect board-state conventions as much as actual work state.
Some chart definitions reference columns or signals that are not fully visible in the summary, limiting root-cause certainty.
Throughput and flow measures reflect completed items only; they do not show item scope changes or rework intensity.
Bug data is broad but does not distinguish severity or customer impact.
